title: Comparative Analysis — Vata vs. Pitta vs. Kapha Doshas
content: A comparative overview of the three doshas highlights their distinct physiological functions, elements, and attributes: 1. Elemental Makeup: Vata is Ether + Air; Pitta is Fire + Water; Kapha is Water + Earth. 2. Primary Role: Vata is Kinetic/Catabolic (movement, nerve transmission, excretion); Pitta is Metabolic/Transformative (digestion, enzymatic reactions, heat); Kapha is Structural/Anabolic (cohesion, growth, lubrication). 3. Thermal Nature: Vata is Cold (Sheeta); Pitta is Hot (Ushna); Kapha is Cold (Sheeta). 4. Moisture Nature: Vata is Dry (Ruksha); Pitta is Lightly Oily (Sasneha); Kapha is Very Oily/Unctuous (Snigdha). 5. Weight/Density: Vata is Light (Laghu); Pitta is Light (Laghu); Kapha is Heavy (Guru). 6. Primary Seat in Body: Vata resides primarily in the colon (Pakwashaya), pelvis, and bones; Pitta resides in the small intestine (Grahani), stomach, and liver; Kapha resides in the chest (Uras), throat, and head.

title: Classical Ayurveda Literature — The Brihat Trayi (Great Triad)
content: The authoritative corpus of classical Ayurveda is anchored in the 'Brihat Trayi' (The Great Three Treatises): 1. Charaka Samhita: Primarily attributed to Acharya Charaka, focusing predominantly on Kaya Chikitsa (internal medicine), foundational philosophy, epistemology, etiology (Nidana), and therapeutics. Emphasizes mind-body balance and lifestyle. 2. Sushruta Samhita: Attributed to Acharya Sushruta, known globally as the pioneer of surgery (Shalya Chikitsa); details surgical procedures, rhinoplasty, anatomical dissections (Sharira), surgical instruments, and trauma management. 3. Ashtanga Hridaya / Ashtanga Sangraha: Composed by Acharya Vagbhata; brilliantly synthesizes and condenses the core teachings of both Charaka and Sushruta into poetic, memorable Sanskrit verses covering all eight clinical branches of Ayurveda (Ashtanga Ayurveda).
source: History of Indian Medicine and AYUSH Research
section: Classical Heritage: Overview of Brihat Trayi

title: The Eight Clinical Branches — Ashtanga Ayurveda
content: Ayurveda traditionally encompasses eight specialized medical branches, termed Ashtanga Ayurveda: 1. Kaya Chikitsa: Internal medicine and general systemic disorders. 2. Shalya Tantra: Surgical techniques, wound care, and foreign body extraction. 3. Shalakya Tantra: Disorders of the ear, nose, throat, eyes, and oral cavity (supraclavicular medicine). 4. Kaumarabhritya: Pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology. 5. Agada Tantra: Toxicology, poisons, and environmental hazards. 6. Rasayana Tantra: Rejuvenation, geriatrics, longevity science, and cellular vitalization. 7. Vajikarana Tantra: Virility, reproductive health, and healthy progeny. 8. Bhuta Vidya (Graha Chikitsa): Psychotherapy and psycho-spiritual health. Together, these branches provided a comprehensive healthcare matrix in classical India.
source: Ministry of AYUSH — Classical Ayurvedic Frameworks
section: Introduction to the Eight Branches of Ayurveda

title: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana: Fundamental Principles of Ayurveda
content: The Charaka Samhita's Sutrasthana (foundational chapter) opens with the definition of Ayurveda: 'Hitahitam sukham duhkham ayustasya hitahitam. Manam cha tachcha yatroktam ayurveda sa uchyate.' — Meaning: That science which defines what is beneficial and harmful, what promotes happiness and unhappiness, and which measures the span of life (Ayu) is called Ayurveda. The text identifies four components of Ayu (life span): Sharira (physical body), Indriya (sensory faculties), Sattva (mind/consciousness), and Atma (soul/self). Charaka Samhita further defines health (Swasthya) as a state where Dosha (physiological forces), Agni (metabolic fire), Dhatu (bodily tissues), Mala (metabolic waste), and Manas (mental equilibrium) are all in their proper functional balance. This text is the foundational textbook for Kaya Chikitsa (internal medicine) in the Ayurvedic tradition.
source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana Chapter 1 (Educational Translation, CCRAS)

title: Sushruta Samhita — Surgical Heritage and Shalya Tantra
content: The Sushruta Samhita, attributed to Acharya Sushruta of Varanasi (~6th century BCE), is among the oldest systematic surgical texts in the world. Key contributions documented within include: 1. Rhinoplasty (nasal reconstruction): The Sushruta Samhita documents detailed procedures for reconstructing the nose using skin flaps from the cheek — predating modern plastic surgery by over 2,500 years. 2. 101 Blunt and 20 sharp surgical instruments (Yantra and Shastra) for various procedures. 3. Formal classifications of wounds (Vrana) and their management including cleaning, debridement, and suturing. 4. Anatomical dissection (Sharira Sthana): Students were required to study cadavers methodically. 5. Classification of diseases into Nija (endogenous) and Agantuja (exogenous/traumatic) origins. The Sushruta Samhita's Nidana Sthana provides systematic disease diagnosis protocols including etiological factors (Nidana), premonitory symptoms (Purvarupa), clinical presentation (Rupa), exploratory therapy (Upashaya), and pathogenesis (Samprapti).

title: Ashtanga Hridaya — Vagbhata's Synthesis of Classical Ayurveda
content: Ashtanga Hridaya Samhita, authored by Acharya Vagbhata (approximately 7th century CE), is the third of the Brihat Trayi and is celebrated for its concise Sanskrit poetry that condenses the teachings of Charaka and Sushruta. The text is divided into six major sections (Sthanas): 1. Sutrasthana (30 chapters): General principles, daily regimen (Dinacharya), seasonal regimen (Ritucharya), and prevention. 2. Sharir Sthana (6 chapters): Embryology, anatomy, and body constitution. 3. Nidana Sthana (16 chapters): Pathology and diagnostics. 4. Chikitsa Sthana (22 chapters): Internal medicine and therapeutics. 5. Kalpa-Siddhi Sthana (6 chapters): Pharmacy and Panchakarma detoxification therapies. 6. Uttara Tantra (40 chapters): Specialized disciplines including ophthalmology, pediatrics, psychiatry, and toxicology. The famous verse 'Swasthasya swasthya rakshanam, aturasya vikara prashamanam' — 'Protecting the health of the healthy, and curing the diseases of the sick' — encapsulates Ayurveda's preventive and curative dual mission.
source: Ashtanga Hridaya Samhita — Sutrasthana (CCRAS Educational Translation)

title: Laghu Trayi — The Minor Classical Triad of Ayurvedic Texts
content: Beyond the Brihat Trayi (Great Triad), Ayurveda recognizes the Laghu Trayi (Minor Triad) of classical texts that provide valuable supplementary knowledge: 1. Madhava Nidana (Roga Vinischaya): Authored by Madhavakara (~8th century CE), this text focuses exclusively on the diagnosis and pathology (Nidana) of diseases and remains widely used in Ayurvedic colleges to this day. It systematically categorizes over 70 disease groups. 2. Sharangadhara Samhita: Written by Sharangadhara (~13th–14th century CE), this text is a pharmacological masterpiece covering preparation of medicines (Kalpana), drug dosing (Matra), pulse diagnosis (Nadi Pariksha), and formulation preparation timings. It introduced pulse examination as a systematic clinical tool in Ayurveda. 3. Bhavaprakasha: Composed by Bhavamishra (~16th century CE), this encyclopedic text updated classical Ayurvedic pharmacopoeia with new herbs, foods, and introduced the concept of 'Haritaki Nighantu' (herbal glossary). It also first described diseases like syphilis (Phirangaroga) encountered from foreign contacts. Together, these six classical texts — the Brihat Trayi and Laghu Trayi — form the canonical foundation of traditional Ayurvedic medical education.
source: Classical Ayurvedic Literature — Ministry of AYUSH Compendium
section: Overview: Laghu Trayi — Minor Classical Texts

title: Panchakarma — The Five Classical Purification Therapies
content: Panchakarma ('Pancha' = five, 'Karma' = action) refers to the five core bio-purification procedures of classical Ayurveda designed to eliminate accumulated doshas and metabolic toxins (Ama) from the body tissues. The five procedures are: 1. Vamana (Therapeutic Emesis): Medicated emesis primarily for Kapha-dominant disorders, respiratory congestion, and skin diseases. Preceded by Snehana (oleation) and Svedana (sudation) preparatory procedures. 2. Virechana (Therapeutic Purgation): Medicated purgation for Pitta-dominant disorders, liver diseases, skin eruptions, and fever. 3. Basti (Medicated Enema): Considered the most effective of all Panchakarma therapies and the primary treatment for Vata disorders. Two types: Anuvasana (oil-based) and Niruha/Asthapana (decoction-based). 4. Nasya (Nasal Administration): Medicated oils or powders administered via the nasal route to treat supra-clavicular disorders, headaches, sinusitis, and neurological conditions. 5. Raktamokshana (Blood-letting/Purification): A specialized procedure for blood-borne diseases (Rakta Vikaras), skin conditions, and localized inflammatory disorders. Panchakarma is always preceded by Purvakarma (preparatory protocols: Snehana and Svedana) and followed by Paschatkarma (post-therapy dietary and lifestyle management).
source: Charaka Samhita — Siddhisthana: Panchakarma Protocols (CCRAS Edition)

title: Sapta Dhatu — The Seven Bodily Tissues of Ayurveda
content: Classical Ayurveda describes the human body as being constituted by seven primary tissue layers (Sapta Dhatu), each sequentially derived from digested food (Ahara Rasa) through the action of each dhatu's own metabolic fire (Dhatvagni): 1. Rasa Dhatu (Plasma/Lymph): The primary nutrient fluid circulating through the body, responsible for nourishment (Preenana) of all subsequent dhatus. 2. Rakta Dhatu (Blood): Specifically the formed blood elements; responsible for life-sustaining (Jeevana) function and oxygen transport. 3. Mamsa Dhatu (Muscle Tissue): Provides physical structure and covering (Lepana) of bones. 4. Meda Dhatu (Adipose/Fat Tissue): Provides lubrication (Snehana) to joints and organs. 5. Asthi Dhatu (Bone Tissue): Provides skeletal support (Dharana) and houses Majja. 6. Majja Dhatu (Bone Marrow / Nervous Tissue): Fills the bone cavities (Purana), nourishes nervous tissue, and produces Shukra. 7. Shukra Dhatu (Reproductive Tissue/Ojas): The most refined dhatu; responsible for reproduction (Garbhotpadana) and ultimately produces Ojas — the vital essence governing immunity and radiance. Each dhatu produces its own waste (Mala) and a refined essence that nurtures the next dhatu in sequence.
source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana Chapter 17: Kiyanta Shiraseeyam (CCRAS)

title: Srotas — The Bodily Channels and Microbiome of Classical Ayurveda
content: Srotas (singular: Srotas; plural: Srotamsi) are the bodily channels, ducts, and micro-circulatory networks through which substances (Dravya), energy, and information flow. Sushruta Samhita enumerates 9 external srotas; Charaka describes 13 internal srotas governing physiological functions: 1. Pranavaha Srotas: Channels for prana (vital breath) — respiratory tract, heart. 2. Udakavaha Srotas: Channels for water/fluid balance — palate, pancreas. 3. Annavaha Srotas: Alimentary/digestive channels — stomach, small intestine. 4. Rasavaha Srotas: Plasma/lymph channels — heart, vessels. 5. Raktavaha Srotas: Blood channels — liver, spleen. 6. Mamsavaha Srotas: Muscle tissue channels — tendons, ligaments. 7. Medovaha Srotas: Fat/lipid channels — kidneys, omentum. 8. Asthivaha Srotas: Bone tissue channels — hip bones, joints. 9. Majjavaha Srotas: Marrow/nerve channels — bone cavities, joints. 10. Shukravaha Srotas: Reproductive tissue channels — testes, ovaries. 11. Purishavaha Srotas: Excretory/fecal channels — colon, rectum. 12. Mutravaha Srotas: Urinary channels — kidneys, bladder. 13. Svedavaha Srotas: Sweat channels — fat tissue, hair follicles. Srotas obstruction (Srotorodha) is a primary pathogenic mechanism leading to disease manifestation.
source: Charaka Samhita — Vimanasthana Chapter 5: Srotovimana (CCRAS Edition)

title: Nidana Panchaka — The Five-Step Diagnostic Framework of Ayurveda
content: The Nidana Panchaka is the classical five-element diagnostic framework codified in the Madhava Nidana and reinforced across the Brihat Trayi, allowing Ayurvedic practitioners to systematically understand disease origin and progression: 1. Nidana (Etiology/Causative Factors): Root causes of disease — Asatmya Indriyartha Samyoga (improper sensory contact), Prajna Paradha (intellectual mistakes/violations of reason), and Parinama (seasonal/temporal changes). 2. Purvarupa (Prodromal Symptoms): Early warning signs appearing before full disease manifestation — subtle, often non-specific indicators that alert to impending doshic imbalance. 3. Rupa (Cardinal Symptoms): The fully manifested clinical signs and symptoms specific to each disease that allow definitive identification. 4. Upashaya (Diagnostic Therapeutic Trial): Using treatments, foods, or environmental changes that relieve or aggravate symptoms as a diagnostic differentiator. 5. Samprapti (Pathogenesis/Disease Mechanism): The complete sequence of disease manifestation — from initial doshic aggravation (Sanchaya), spread (Prasara), localization (Sthanasamshraya), manifestation (Vyakti), to chronicity (Bheda). The Samprapti unfolds through the six stages (Shat Kriyakala) of disease progression.
source: Madhava Nidana — Roga Vinischaya: Diagnostic Framework (CCRAS Edition)

title: Rasayana Tantra — Classical Rejuvenation and Anti-Aging Science
content: Rasayana Tantra is one of the eight branches of Ashtanga Ayurveda, dedicated entirely to rejuvenation, longevity, and cellular revitalization. The term 'Rasayana' derives from 'Rasa' (essence, plasma, the first dhatu) + 'Ayana' (pathway/channel) — literally 'the path to refined essence.' Classical Charaka Samhita (Chikitsa Sthana, Chapter 1) defines Rasayana as therapies that promote: Dirghamayushyam (long lifespan), Medhya (intellect/memory enhancement), Balyam (physical and immune strength), Arogya (freedom from disease), Yauvanam (youthful vitality), Prabha (complexion/lustre), and Svara-Varna Sampat (quality of voice and complexion). Classical Rasayana herbs include: Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica) — considered the supreme Rasayana; Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) — Medhya and Balya Rasayana; Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) — Jeevaniya and female reproductive Rasayana; Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) — Medhya Rasayana for cognitive function; Haritaki (Terminalia chebula) — known as the 'mother of all herbs,' pacifies all three doshas. Kutipraveshika Rasayana (indoor chamber rejuvenation) and Vatatapika Rasayana (outdoor ambulatory) are the two main procedural modes described in classical texts.
source: Charaka Samhita — Chikitsasthana Chapter 1: Rasayana Pada (CCRAS Edition)

title: Agni — The Metabolic Fire and Its Four States in Ayurveda
content: Agni (metabolic fire) is considered the central pillar of health in classical Ayurveda — 'Agni eva ayuh' (Agni is life itself), states the Ashtanga Hridaya. The primary Agni of the body is Jatharagni (digestive fire, located in the stomach and small intestine), which governs the transformation of ingested food into nutrients. Jatharagni manifests in four clinical states: 1. Sama Agni (Balanced Fire): Optimal digestion and metabolism; the hallmark of health (Swasthya). Digests food in appropriate time without discomfort, produces nourishing Rasa. 2. Vishama Agni (Irregular/Variable Fire): Associated with Vata imbalance; results in erratic digestion, alternating constipation and loose stools, gas, bloating, and variable appetite. 3. Tikshna Agni (Sharp/Hyperactive Fire): Associated with Pitta aggravation; manifests as excessive hunger, heartburn, acid reflux, inflammation, and rapid but incomplete digestion. 4. Manda Agni (Slow/Sluggish Fire): Associated with Kapha dominance; manifests as slow digestion, heavy feeling after meals, sluggishness, weight gain, and mucus production. Beyond Jatharagni, classical texts identify 5 Bhutagnis (elemental fires) and 7 Dhatvagnis (tissue-specific metabolic fires), forming a hierarchical metabolic system governing the sequential transformation and nourishment of the Sapta Dhatu.
source: Ashtanga Hridaya — Sutrasthana Chapter 13: Doshabhediya Adhyaya (CCRAS)

title: Ojas — The Vital Essence and Immunity in Classical Ayurveda
content: Ojas is the quintessential vital essence of life in classical Ayurveda — the most refined product of optimal digestion, dhatu nourishment, and spiritual practice. Charaka Samhita (Sutrasthana, Chapter 17) describes Ojas as existing in two forms: 1. Para Ojas (Supreme Ojas): Eight drops (Asta Bindava) located in the heart (Hridaya), considered the seat of consciousness and the ultimate life force. Its complete destruction causes death. 2. Apara Ojas (Secondary Ojas): Half an Anjali measure (approximately 100ml) distributed throughout the body, equivalent to the immune system and overall vitality. Ojas is pale yellow, slightly oily, cool, and sweet in nature. Classical qualities (Gunas) of Ojas include: Guru (heavy), Sheeta (cool), Mrudu (soft), Snigdha (unctuous), Bahula (abundant), Vishada (clear), Picchila (slightly viscous), and Madhura (sweet). Factors that deplete Ojas (Ojokshaya) include: Excessive physical exertion, starvation, grief, anger, excessive sexual activity, trauma, and chronic disease. Ojas is enhanced by Rasayana therapy, sattvic diet, pranayama, meditation, and deep restorative sleep (Nidra). Modern interpretation connects Ojas to innate immune resilience, hormonal vitality, and psycho-neuro-immunological balance.
source: Charaka Samhita — Sutrasthana Chapter 17 (CCRAS Educational Edition)

title: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) — Overview and Authority
content: The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) is the official compendium published by the Government of India, Ministry of AYUSH, establishing quality standards for single Ayurvedic drugs. The API serves as the primary regulatory and educational reference for: 1. Botanical Identity Verification: Official botanical name, family, and part used for each medicinal plant. 2. Macroscopic and Microscopic Characteristics: Visual and histological identification standards. 3. Chemical Constituents: Key phytochemical markers used for standardization. 4. Tests for Quality: Ash values, extractive values, moisture content, and limit tests. 5. Identification Tests: Thin-Layer Chromatography (TLC) profiles and chemical color reactions. 6. Assay Methods: Quantitative standards for active principles. The API is published in multiple volumes covering both Part I (single drugs) and Part II (formulations). Key monographs include Tulsi, Ashwagandha, Haritaki, Shatavari, Brahmi, Guduchi, Nimba, Yashtimadhu, and hundreds of additional herbs. All AyurBot corpus citations from the API are sourced directly from these official AYUSH publications to ensure authenticity and regulatory compliance.
source: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India (API) — Ministry of AYUSH, Government of India
